If something you need isn't here or in module avail, see Request Software or Install Software Yourself.

docs.title: Storage Locations and Quotas
docs.text:
Each place you can keep files on FarmShare has its own size limit and rules for how long files stay.

Location Path Size limit Backed up Cleared out Available on Home ~ (/home/users/$USER) 50 GB Short-term Never All nodes Scratch /scratch/users/$USER None No Files not modified in 90 days All nodes Class and group home /home/classes, /home/groups On request Ask us Ask us All nodes Class and group scratch /scratch/classes, /scratch/groups On request No Ask us All nodes Local temporary /tmp Node's local disk No When the job ends Each node, separately AFS ~/afs-home, /afs Managed by University IT Managed by University IT Never Login nodes only

Needs Review

Is scratch space backed up at all? The admin draft only says home directories are backed up for a short time.

Home is for things you want to keep: code, scripts, configuration files, small data sets and results. Scratch is for working data that doesn't fit in home. Copy anything you need to keep out of scratch before it's cleared, to home or to Oak. Only home directories are backed up.

$SCRATCH isn't set on FarmShare. Use the full path, /scratch/users/$USER.

There's no quota command. df shows the size of the whole shared file system, not your share of it, so check your usage with du:

du -sh ~

du reports sizes in GiB, so a full home directory shows as about 48G.

On compute nodes, /tmp belongs to the running job and is deleted when the job ends. On login nodes, it's cleared often.

Class and group directories are set up on request. See Set Up a Course or email srcc-support@stanford.edu.

For how to choose among these, see Where to Put Your Files. For AFS, see Use AFS.

docs.title: Additional Resources
docs.text: When your work doesn't fit on FarmShare, one of these services may. Some are run by Stanford Research Computing, and some are outside it.

docs.title: Other Stanford Research Computing Services
docs.text: Page What it covers Sherlock The cluster for sponsored and departmental research Oak Long-term storage for research groups Nero A Google Cloud environment for high-risk data Carina A secure computing environment for high-risk data Marlowe A large GPU cluster for AI and other research

docs.title: Outside Stanford Research Computing
docs.text: Page What it covers NSF ACCESS Time on national computing systems Google Cloud Commercial cloud computing, and the ways to get it at Stanford

docs.title: Carina
docs.text: Carina is a secure computing environment approved for high-risk data. Stanford Research Computing runs it, like FarmShare, but it's a separate system with its own accounts and documentation.

docs.title: When to Use Carina Instead
docs.text: FarmShare can't be used for high-risk data, such as protected health information or personally identifiable information. If your work involves high-risk data, use Carina or Nero. See Stanford's data risk classifications to check how your data is classified.

docs.title: Getting Access
docs.text: See the Carina documentation for how to request access.

docs.title: Google Cloud
docs.text: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is a commercial cloud service you can use for computing when FarmShare isn't the right fit. There are a few ways to get it at Stanford. None of them is a Stanford Research Computing service, except Nero, which is described below.

docs.title: When Google Cloud Is Useful
docs.text: Cloud computing lets you pay for exactly the machines you need, when you need them, including GPU types and memory sizes FarmShare doesn't have. You're billed for what you use, so it suits work that's short, irregular, or needs something specific. For work that fits within FarmShare's limits, FarmShare is free.

docs.title: Stanford GCP Projects
docs.text:
University IT runs Stanford's Google Cloud accounts. A Stanford GCP project comes under Stanford's agreements with Google, and you log in with your SUNet ID. It's billed to a Stanford PTA, so you need approval from someone who can approve charges to that PTA before you request a project.

See University IT's Guide to Stanford GCP Setup for how to request a project. Questions go to University IT, not to us.

docs.title: Google Cloud for Courses
docs.text: Google offers education credits that instructors can apply for to teach a course with Google Cloud. The credits go into a billing account for the course. See Google Cloud for Education for eligibility and how to apply.

docs.title: Personal Google Cloud Accounts
docs.text: You can also sign up for Google Cloud yourself with a personal account and pay Google directly. A personal account isn't a Stanford project, so it isn't covered by Stanford's agreements with Google. Don't use one for Stanford data unless you've checked that it's allowed for that data.

docs.title: High-Risk Data
docs.text: FarmShare can't be used for high-risk data. Stanford's guidance is that high-risk data on Google Cloud has to be managed by an authorized group, such as Stanford Research Computing. Nero is SRC's Google Cloud environment for high-risk data, and it's the place to start if your work involves it.

docs.title: Marlowe
docs.text: Marlowe is a large GPU cluster for AI and other research that needs specialized hardware. Stanford Research Computing runs it, like FarmShare, but it's a separate system with its own accounts and documentation.

docs.title: When to Use Marlowe Instead
docs.text: FarmShare has 6 GPU nodes, and each person can use up to 4 GPUs at a time. That's enough for learning and for smaller models. If your research needs many GPUs for large-scale AI work, look at Marlowe.

docs.title: Getting Access
docs.text: Access to Marlowe is through project applications. See the Marlowe documentation for how to apply.

docs.title: Nero
docs.text: Nero is a cloud computing environment and big data platform for high-risk data, built on Google Cloud. Stanford Research Computing runs it, like FarmShare, but it's a separate system with its own accounts and documentation.

docs.title: When to Use Nero Instead
docs.text: FarmShare can't be used for high-risk data, such as protected health information or personally identifiable information. If your work involves high-risk data and fits a cloud environment, use Nero. For an on-premises option, see Carina.

docs.title: Getting Access
docs.text: See the Nero documentation for how to request access.

docs.title: NSF ACCESS
docs.text: NSF ACCESS is a national program, funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation, that gives researchers and educators time on supercomputers and other computing systems at institutions around the country. It isn't run by Stanford Research Computing.

docs.title: When ACCESS Is Useful
docs.text:
ACCESS is an option when your work needs more computing than FarmShare's limits allow, or hardware FarmShare doesn't have, and it doesn't fit on Sherlock. Allocations are free to the people who receive them.

It's also used for teaching. The smaller project types are meant for classes and training events as well as research.

docs.title: Allocation Types
docs.text:
ACCESS has four project types, from small to large:

Type Meant for Review Explore Trying out resources, graduate student projects, small classes Short request, checked for eligibility Discover Research with modest needs, graduate student projects, large classes Short request, checked for eligibility Accelerate Experienced researchers with mid-scale needs Longer proposal with panel review Maximize Large-scale research Full proposal with panel review, twice a year

The ACCESS project types page gives the credit limits and proposal lengths for each.

docs.title: Who Can Apply
docs.text:
To lead an ACCESS project, you have to be a U.S.-based researcher or educator, at the graduate student level or higher. Graduate students can lead Explore and Discover projects, and their advisor has to be part of the request. Undergraduates can't lead a project, but they can work on one led by an eligible advisor or instructor. Instructors can lead projects for their classes.

The ACCESS allocations policy has the full rules.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Create an ACCESS account with your Stanford email address, then request an allocation. See ACCESS for graduate students and ACCESS Allocations for the steps.

docs.title: Oak
docs.text: Oak is Stanford Research Computing's long-term storage service for research groups. It's a separate service from FarmShare, with its own documentation, and it isn't mounted on FarmShare.

docs.title: When Oak Is Useful
docs.text:
FarmShare has no long-term storage beyond your home directory, and scratch files are deleted after 90 days without changes. Oak is for research data that a group needs to keep and share over the long term.

Because Oak isn't mounted on FarmShare, you can't use files on Oak directly in a FarmShare job. Copy the data you need into your scratch directory, /scratch/users/$USER, with rsync or Globus, and copy results back when the work is done. See Move Files to and from FarmShare.

Oak can hold low- and moderate-risk data, but not high-risk data. It isn't backed up unless the group adds backups.

docs.title: Getting Oak Storage
docs.text:
A faculty member or PI rents Oak space for their group, month to month. Ask your advisor or PI whether your group already has space. Current prices are on University IT's Research Computing Storage Rates page.

See the Oak documentation to get started.

docs.title: Sherlock
docs.text: Sherlock is Stanford's large shared computing cluster for faculty and their research groups. Stanford Research Computing runs it, like FarmShare, but it's a separate system with its own accounts, storage and documentation.

docs.title: When to Use Sherlock Instead
docs.text:
FarmShare is for coursework and unsponsored research. Sherlock is the better fit when:

  • your research is sponsored, or funded by a grant or department
  • your jobs need more than FarmShare's limits allow, such as more memory than a FarmShare job can use
  • your group needs shared storage that lasts beyond a single course

Sherlock isn't meant for coursework or class assignments, so course projects stay on FarmShare.

docs.title: Getting an Account
docs.text:
A faculty member sponsors Sherlock accounts for their group, so ask your advisor or PI to request one for you. Any SUNet ID can be used.

See the Sherlock documentation to get started.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Much of the software on FarmShare is installed as modules, and you can install more yourself in your home directory. For something neither covers, ask us.

Page What it covers Find Installed Software Finding and loading modules Request Software Asking us to install software Python Python versions and virtual environments with uv R R, your personal package library, and renv Conda-Style Environments Pixi and Micromamba for packages from conda-forge Install Software Yourself Package managers and building from source without administrator rights Containers Running containers with Apptainer and Podman AI Coding Agents Installing and running tools such as Claude Code and Codex CLI Licensed Software Commercial programs licensed on FarmShare, such as MATLAB, Stata and Ansys

docs.title: AI Coding Agents
docs.text: AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI aren't installed on FarmShare, and there are no modules for them. You can install them yourself in your home directory, the same way you'd install other software without administrator rights.

docs.title: Install an Agent
docs.text:
Use the install instructions from the tool's own documentation, and choose the option for installing as a regular user on Linux. Most agents offer either a standalone installer or a package from npm.

Installers that put files in your home directory, such as under ~/.local, work without administrator rights. Instructions that start with sudo won't work on FarmShare. If a tool needs Node.js, check whether it's installed as a module:

module spider nodejs

For general advice on installing software without administrator rights, see Install Software Yourself.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
We don't block the Anthropic, OpenAI or other AI service APIs on FarmShare, so agents that connect to them can run here. That isn't a promise that a particular tool will work, and we can't promise to fix problems with the tools themselves. You need your own account or API key with the service, and you're responsible for its costs.

Agents, their caches and the files they create are stored in your home directory and count toward your 50 GB home quota. Some keep large logs or caches, so check them with du if your home directory fills up. See Check and Free Up Space.

You can run an agent on a login node for editing and small tasks. If it runs heavy work, such as training a model or a long test suite, run that work on a compute node in an interactive session or a batch job.

An agent sends your code and files to an outside service. FarmShare isn't approved for high-risk data, and you shouldn't send data to an AI service unless Stanford's rules for that data allow it. See Policy.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: If an agent can't connect, or hangs the next time you start it, save the full error output. Check the tool's own documentation and issue tracker first. If it looks like a FarmShare problem, such as a network connection that fails only on FarmShare, ask us and include the error.

docs.title: Conda-Style Environments
docs.text: Pixi and Micromamba create environments from conda-forge packages. Unlike plain Python or R environments, they can also install the non-Python and non-R libraries that some packages depend on, such as C libraries. Use them when a package won't install with pip, uv or install.packages().

docs.title: Micromamba
docs.text:
Micromamba is available as a module:

module load micromamba
micromamba create -n myenv -c conda-forge python numpy
micromamba activate myenv

Micromamba uses the same commands as conda, so most conda instructions work if you replace conda with micromamba.

docs.title: Pixi
docs.text:
Pixi keeps an environment inside a project folder and records its packages in a file you can share. To use it, install it in your home directory with the Pixi installer:

pixi init myproject
cd myproject
pixi add python numpy
pixi run python analysis.py

docs.title: Use an Environment in a Batch Job
docs.text:
Activate the environment in the script, the same way you do by hand. For Micromamba:

module load micromamba
micromamba activate myenv
python3 analysis.py

For Pixi, run commands through pixi run from the project folder.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text: Environments and their package caches live in your home directory and count toward your 50 GB quota. They grow quickly. Remove environments you're done with, and clear old downloads with micromamba clean --all or pixi clean cache.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: A container bundles a program with everything it needs to run, so it works the same way on FarmShare as on the computer where it was built. FarmShare has two container tools: Apptainer, which is the usual choice for jobs, and Podman, which works like Docker. Docker itself isn't available.

docs.title: Apptainer
docs.text:
Load the module, then pull an image from a registry such as Docker Hub:

module load apptainer
apptainer pull docker://ubuntu:24.04

This creates an image file, ubuntu_24.04.sif, in the current directory. Run commands inside it with apptainer exec:

apptainer exec ubuntu_24.04.sif cat /etc/os-release
Command What it does apptainer pull Downloads an image from a registry and saves it as a .sif file apptainer run Runs the image's default command apptainer exec Runs a command you choose inside the image apptainer shell Opens an interactive shell inside the image

In a batch job, load the module and call apptainer exec in the script. Apptainer was formerly called Singularity, and most Singularity instructions still work.

docs.title: Podman
docs.text:
Podman uses the same commands as Docker, so instructions written for Docker usually work if you replace docker with podman:

podman run --rm docker.io/library/ubuntu:24.04 cat /etc/os-release

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
Container images are large. Keep .sif files in your scratch directory (/scratch/users/$USER) rather than your home directory, and keep a copy of any image you can't download again, since scratch files are cleared out after 90 days without changes.

To share an image with a class, instructors can ask us to put it in the class directory. See Set Up a Course.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: See Software and Modules.

docs.title: Install Software Yourself
docs.text: You can install your own software on FarmShare, in your home directory or in a class or group directory. You can't install system packages with sudo or apt. If you need one, ask us.

docs.title: Use a Package Manager
docs.text:
A package manager is usually the easiest way to install software without administrator rights:

Package manager Good for uv Python packages. See Python. Pixi or Micromamba Anything on conda-forge, including libraries other packages depend on. See Conda-Style Environments. Spack Scientific and HPC software built from source

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
Most software that builds with ./configure and make, or with CMake, can be installed in your home directory by setting the install location:

./configure --prefix=$HOME/software/myprogram
make
make install

Then add its bin folder to your path, for example in ~/.bashrc:

export PATH=$HOME/software/myprogram/bin:$PATH

Compilers and build tools are available as modules. See Find Installed Software.

docs.title: Software for a Class or Group
docs.text: Classes and groups can install shared software in their own directories, so everyone uses the same copy. See Set Up a Course for getting a class directory. For software many classes use, ask us to install it as a module instead.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
Software you install counts toward the quota of the directory it's in, and your home directory holds 50 GB. Programs with a graphical interface need a desktop session to run.

If a program needs Docker, see Containers.

docs.title: Find Installed Software
docs.text: Software on FarmShare comes from two places. Common tools are installed as part of the operating system and work as soon as you log in. Specialized and newer software is provided as modules, which you load when you need them.

docs.title: Software That's Already There
docs.text:
The operating system, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, includes many standard tools. Run them directly:

python3 --version

Python 3.12.3

docs.title: Load a Module
docs.text:
Modules give you software that isn't in the operating system, or a newer or specially built version of something that is. Loading a module sets up your environment so the software is found:

module load python
python3 --version

Python 3.14.2

Loading a module only affects your current session. In a batch job, load the modules the job needs inside the script.

ml is a shorter way to type module. ml python does the same thing as module load python.

docs.title: Find Software
docs.text:
To list every module, run:

module avail

To search for a module by name, use module spider. It also finds modules that module avail doesn't show until something else is loaded:

module spider cuda

To search module names and descriptions for a word, use module keyword:

module keyword chemistry

Some modules have more than one version. Without a version, module load picks the default. To choose one, name it, for example module load cuda/12.9.0.

docs.title: Letters in module avail
docs.text: Letter Meaning D The default version, loaded when you don't name one L Currently loaded g Built for GPUs; use it in jobs on the GPU nodes S Sticky; module purge leaves it loaded unless you add --force

docs.title: Module Commands
docs.text:
Command Short form What it does module avail ml av Lists available software module spider <name> ml spider <name> Searches for software by name module keyword <word> ml key <word> Searches names and descriptions module whatis <name> ml whatis <name> Shows a short description module help <name> ml help <name> Shows help for a module module load <name> ml <name> Loads a module module unload <name> ml -<name> Unloads a module module list ml Lists loaded modules module purge ml purge Unloads all modules module save <set> ml save <set> Saves the loaded modules as a named set module restore <set> ml restore <set> Loads a saved set

FarmShare uses Lmod. Its user guide covers the rest.

docs.title: If It Isn't Here
docs.text: You can install software yourself, or ask us to add it.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: FarmShare has two versions of Python. The operating system's python3 is version 3.12.3, and module load python gives you 3.14.2. For your own packages, use a virtual environment. We recommend creating and managing them with uv.

docs.title: Create a Virtual Environment with uv
docs.text:
A virtual environment is a folder holding its own Python packages, separate from everyone else's and from your other projects. uv creates them quickly and stores packages efficiently, which helps with the 50 GB home quota.

uv venv ~/myproject
source ~/myproject/bin/activate
uv pip install numpy

This creates the environment in your home directory, at ~/myproject. source ~/myproject/bin/activate switches your shell to that environment, and your prompt starts with (myproject). Run deactivate to leave it.

uv can also create environments with a specific Python version, for example uv venv --python 3.12 ~/myproject.

If the uv command isn't found, install it in your home directory with the standalone installer. It doesn't need administrator rights.

docs.title: Use the Standard Tools Instead
docs.text:
Python's own venv and pip also work:

module load python
python3 -m venv ~/myproject
source ~/myproject/bin/activate
pip install numpy

docs.title: Use an Environment in a Batch Job
docs.text:
Activate the environment in the script before running Python:

python-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=python-example
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

source ~/myproject/bin/activate
python3 analysis.py

If you created the environment with module load python loaded, as in the standard-tools example above, add module load python to the script too, before the source line.

docs.title: Use an Environment in JupyterLab
docs.text:
To use an environment's packages in the JupyterLab app in OnDemand, install it as a Jupyter kernel:

source ~/myproject/bin/activate
uv pip install ipykernel
python3 -m ipykernel install --user --name myproject

The next time you open JupyterLab, myproject appears in the list of kernels.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
Environments and package caches live in your home directory and count toward your 50 GB quota. Machine learning packages are large, so a few environments can fill it. Delete environments you no longer use, and clear old downloads with uv cache clean or pip cache purge.

For packages that need non-Python libraries, see Conda-Style Environments.

docs.title: R
docs.text: R is available as a module, and in the RStudio app in OnDemand. Packages you install go into a personal library in your home directory.

docs.title: Start R
docs.text:
ml r
R

docs.title: Install Packages
docs.text:
install.packages("dplyr")

The shared R library isn't writable, so R installs packages into a personal library in your home directory instead. The first time you install a package, R asks whether to create one. Answer yes.

Packages you install from a terminal are also available in RStudio, and the other way around.

Some packages fail to install from inside RStudio but install fine from R in a terminal. If an install fails in RStudio, try it from a terminal first.

docs.title: Keep Project Environments with renv
docs.text:
renv records the exact packages a project uses, so you can recreate its environment later or share it:

install.packages("renv")
renv::init()

See the renv documentation for more.

docs.title: Packages That Need System Libraries
docs.text: Some R packages depend on libraries written in other languages, such as C. If an install fails because a library is missing, you can use Pixi or Micromamba, which install those libraries alongside R. Or ask us to add the library, and include the package name and the full error.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text: Your personal library counts toward your 50 GB home quota.

docs.title: Request Software
docs.text: If software you need isn't on FarmShare, we may be able to install it. We add software that's useful to many people, either as a module or as a system package. For something only you need, it's usually faster to install it yourself.

docs.title: Check First
docs.text:
Search the modules before you ask:

module spider <name>

Some software is installed as part of the operating system and isn't a module. Try running the command directly, or check with which <name>.

docs.title: Ask Us
docs.text:
Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject, and include:

  1. The name of the software and a link to its website.
  2. The version you need, if it matters.
  3. What you're using it for, such as a course or a research project.
  4. Whether it needs a license.

docs.title: Software for a Course
docs.text: Instructors who need software for a class should ask well before the quarter starts, since installing and testing takes time. Include the course number and roughly how many students will use it. See Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

docs.title: Licensed Software
docs.text: Some commercial software, such as MATLAB, Gaussian, Stata and Ansys, is already licensed on FarmShare. See Licensed Software for what's available and how to use it. For software that isn't licensed yet, include who is paying for the license in your request.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Stanford licenses several commercial programs for use on FarmShare. You don't need to buy or activate anything yourself. Load the program's module and it finds the license on its own.

docs.title: What's Licensed
docs.text:
Software Module Usually run Page MATLAB matlab OnDemand MATLAB app, or batch jobs MATLAB Gaussian and GaussView gaussian GaussView in a desktop, Gaussian in batch jobs Gaussian and GaussView Stata stata Interactive session or batch jobs Stata Ansys, including HFSS ansys FarmShare Desktop Ansys and HFSS SAS sas Batch jobs SAS Mathematica mathematica Desktop, or scripts in batch jobs Mathematica Gurobi gurobi Batch jobs Gurobi Schrödinger schrodinger Desktop Schrödinger Sentaurus Provided by EE Caddyshack Desktop Sentaurus

Versions change when licenses are renewed. To see which versions are installed now, run module spider with the module name:

module spider matlab

docs.title: Who Can Use It
docs.text:
Anyone with a FarmShare account can use the licensed software, for the same work FarmShare is for: coursework and unsponsored research. If your research is sponsored, use Sherlock instead. Sentaurus is the exception. It's licensed and supported by Electrical Engineering, not by us.

Licenses are shared by everyone on FarmShare, and some allow only a limited number of people to run the program at once. If a program says it can't get a license, the licenses may all be in use. Try again a little later, and if it keeps happening, let us know.

docs.title: Programs with a Graphical Interface
docs.text:
Programs with a graphical interface, such as GaussView or the Ansys Electronics Desktop, run in a FarmShare Desktop. Start a desktop in OnDemand, open a terminal in it, load the module and start the program. See Run GUI Programs.

Everything you start in a desktop stops when the desktop session ends, including calculations that are still running. For long calculations, submit a batch job instead.

docs.title: Licensed Software for a Course
docs.text:
If your course needs one of these packages, say so when you ask for your course setup, so we can check that it's installed and working before the quarter starts. If the course needs software that isn't licensed on FarmShare yet, ask as early as you can and say who will pay for the license. A new license takes much longer to arrange than installing free software. See Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

For other software, see Request Software.

docs.title: Ansys and HFSS
docs.text:
Needs Review

Is Ansys on FarmShare licensed for teaching only, or also for unsponsored research? Confirm with UIT Software Licensing.

Ansys is licensed on FarmShare for coursework. If you want to use it for research, ask us first. The ansys module includes the Ansys Electronics Desktop, which contains HFSS. Run it in a FarmShare Desktop.

docs.title: Start the Electronics Desktop
docs.text:
Before you start: start a FarmShare Desktop in OnDemand. See Run GUI Programs.

Open a terminal in the desktop and run:

module load ansys
ansysedt &

The & lets you keep using the terminal while the Electronics Desktop is open. HFSS is in the Electronics Desktop's project menus.

To see which Ansys versions are installed, run module spider ansys. To see what else the module provides, run module help ansys.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
The Electronics Desktop runs inside your desktop session, and so do the simulations you start from it. When the session ends, they stop. Choose a session length that covers the simulation, and save your project before the session runs out.

If you're using Ansys for sponsored research, use your group's own license on Sherlock instead.

docs.title: Teaching with Ansys
docs.text:
For a class tutorial, have each student start their own FarmShare Desktop and run Ansys there. Don't have a whole class run it from the FarmShare Shell Access terminal in OnDemand. That terminal always opens on the same login node, and fifty copies of Ansys on one login node run slowly for everyone.

Mention Ansys in your course setup request so we can check it before the class. See Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

docs.title: The Electronics Desktop Crashes When I Save a Project
docs.text:
The Electronics Desktop has had trouble saving projects to network file systems, which include your home directory. When this happens, it crashes with an error like Aborted (core dumped), sometimes after Path is too long.

To work around it, set the project directory to a folder in /tmp, which is on the node's own disk. In the Electronics Desktop, go to Tools > Options > General Options > General > Directories and set the project directory to /tmp/$USER (with your SUNet ID in place of $USER).

/tmp is on the node your desktop runs on, and it's deleted when the session ends. Before the session ends, copy your project to your home or scratch directory:

cp -r /tmp/$USER/myproject ~/

If the crash happens somewhere other than saving, tell us what you were doing when it crashed.

docs.title: Gaussian and GaussView
docs.text: Gaussian and its graphical interface, GaussView, are licensed on FarmShare and are used in chemistry courses. Both come from the gaussian module. Use GaussView in a FarmShare Desktop to build molecules and look at results, and run longer calculations as batch jobs.

docs.title: Use GaussView
docs.text:
Before you start: start a FarmShare Desktop in OnDemand. See Run GUI Programs.

Open a terminal in the desktop and run:

module load gaussian
gv

GaussView also works over SSH with display forwarding (ssh -X), but a desktop is faster and more reliable.

Calculations you start from GaussView run inside the desktop session, and they stop when the session ends. That's fine for short calculations. For anything that might outlast the session, save the input file and submit it as a batch job.

docs.title: Run Gaussian in a Batch Job
docs.text:
gaussian-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gaussian    # (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8      # (2)
#SBATCH --mem=16G              # (3)
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00        # (4)

module load gaussian           # (5)
g16 molecule.gjf               # (6)
  1. A name for the job, shown in squeue.
  2. How many CPU cores the job gets. Set %NProcShared in your input file to the same number.
  3. How much memory the job gets. Set %Mem in your input file a little lower, so Gaussian stays inside the job's limit.
  4. How long the job can run. Jobs can run for up to 2 days.
  5. Loads the default Gaussian version. Run module spider gaussian to see the others.
  6. Runs Gaussian 16 on the input file. The output goes to molecule.log.

Submit it with sbatch gaussian-job.sh. See Submit a Batch Job.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
If a whole class opens desktops for Gaussian at once, choose the smallest desktop size and shortest time that fit the work. Desktops share the same nodes, and smaller requests start sooner for everyone. Close the desktop when you're done rather than leaving it to run out.

Instructors planning to use Gaussian in a course should say so in their course setup request. See Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

docs.title: Gurobi
docs.text: The Gurobi optimizer is one of the commercial packages installed on FarmShare. It's provided as the gurobi module. If Gurobi reports a license error when you run it, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject and include the message.

docs.title: Use Gurobi
docs.text:
Load the module before you run Gurobi, whether from its own command line or from Python:

module load gurobi
gurobi_cl model.lp

Run module spider gurobi to see the installed versions. If you use gurobipy from Python, install the gurobipy version that matches the module's Gurobi version.

In a batch job, put module load gurobi in the script before the command that runs Gurobi. See Submit a Batch Job.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text: Don't use a free academic license tied to your own computer. Those licenses check which computer they're running on, and your jobs run on different FarmShare nodes each time, so they fail with a host ID error.

docs.title: Mathematica
docs.text: Mathematica is licensed on FarmShare and comes from the mathematica module. Use notebooks in a FarmShare Desktop, or run Wolfram Language scripts as batch jobs.

docs.title: Use Notebooks
docs.text:
Before you start: start a FarmShare Desktop in OnDemand. See Run GUI Programs.

Open a terminal in the desktop and run:

module load mathematica
mathematica &

docs.title: Run a Script in a Batch Job
docs.text:
Save your code as a .wls script and run it with wolframscript:

mathematica-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mathematica    # (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1         # (2)
#SBATCH --mem=8G                  # (3)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00           # (4)

module load mathematica           # (5)
wolframscript -file analysis.wls  # (6)
  1. A name for the job, shown in squeue.
  2. How many CPU cores the job gets.
  3. How much memory the job gets.
  4. How long the job can run, as hours:minutes:seconds.
  5. Loads the default Mathematica version. Run module spider mathematica to see the others.
  6. Runs the script without a notebook.

Submit it with sbatch mathematica-job.sh. See Submit a Batch Job.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: If Mathematica says it isn't activated or can't find a license, the license server may be having trouble. It isn't something you can fix by activating your own copy. Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject and include the message.

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text: MATLAB is licensed on FarmShare for everyone with an account. The easiest way to use it is the MATLAB app in OnDemand, which opens the full MATLAB desktop in your browser. For longer work, run MATLAB scripts as batch jobs.

docs.title: Use the MATLAB App
docs.text:
1. Go to OnDemand.
  2. Select Interactive Apps > MATLAB.
  3. Choose how long you need and select Launch.
  4. When the session is ready, select the button to connect.

The session ends at the time you chose, and MATLAB closes with it. Save your work to your home or scratch directory as you go.

docs.title: Run MATLAB in a Batch Job
docs.text:
Write your code as a script or function file, then call it with matlab -batch. This example runs analysis.m from the directory you submit the job from:

matlab-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=matlab-example    # (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4            # (2)
#SBATCH --mem=16G                    # (3)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00              # (4)

module load matlab                   # (5)
matlab -batch "analysis"             # (6)
  1. A name for the job, shown in squeue.
  2. How many CPU cores the job gets. Parallel code such as parfor can use up to this many workers.
  3. How much memory the job gets. MATLAB uses a good deal of memory to start, so allow more than your data alone needs.
  4. How long the job can run, as hours:minutes:seconds.
  5. Loads the default MATLAB version. Run module spider matlab to see the others.
  6. Runs analysis.m without the graphical interface, then exits. Use the script's name without .m.

Submit it with sbatch matlab-job.sh. See Submit a Batch Job for more about batch jobs.

docs.title: Run MATLAB from a Terminal
docs.text:
For the MATLAB desktop, use the MATLAB app. In an SSH session or an interactive session, you can start MATLAB without the graphical interface:

module load matlab
matlab -nodisplay

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
When MATLAB starts from a terminal, it may print MATLAB is selecting SOFTWARE OPENGL rendering. That message on its own isn't an error. If MATLAB doesn't open after it, use the MATLAB app instead.

Add-on toolboxes are whatever the license includes. To see them, run ver at the MATLAB prompt.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: See OnDemand and Desktops for problems starting the app, and Software and Modules for problems with the module.

docs.title: SAS
docs.text: SAS is licensed on FarmShare and comes from the sas module. Run SAS programs as batch jobs, or from an interactive session.

docs.title: Run a SAS Program
docs.text:
sas-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=sas         # (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1      # (2)
#SBATCH --mem=8G               # (3)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00        # (4)

module load sas                # (5)
sas analysis.sas               # (6)
  1. A name for the job, shown in squeue.
  2. How many CPU cores the job gets.
  3. How much memory the job gets.
  4. How long the job can run, as hours:minutes:seconds.
  5. Loads SAS. Run module spider sas to see the installed versions.
  6. Runs analysis.sas. SAS writes its log to analysis.log and its output to analysis.lst.

Submit it with sbatch sas-job.sh. See Submit a Batch Job.

To run the same commands interactively, start an interactive session first.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: If the module won't load or SAS reports a license problem, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject and include the full error.

docs.title: Schrödinger
docs.text: The Schrödinger suite, including Maestro, is licensed on FarmShare and comes from the schrodinger module. Run Maestro in a FarmShare Desktop.

docs.title: Start Maestro
docs.text:
Before you start: start a FarmShare Desktop in OnDemand. See Run GUI Programs.

Open a terminal in the desktop and run:

module load schrodinger
maestro &

Run module spider schrodinger to see the installed versions. Some Schrödinger tools can use GPUs. See Use GPUs for how to get one.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
Jobs you start from Maestro in a desktop stop when the desktop session ends. Choose a session length that covers them.

If a tool reports that the license doesn't include it, or that no license is available, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject and include the tool's name and the message.

docs.title: Sentaurus
docs.text: Sentaurus is Synopsys TCAD software used in Electrical Engineering courses and research. On FarmShare it's provided, licensed and supported by EE, not by Stanford Research Computing. You run it from a Caddyshack Desktop.

docs.title: Run Sentaurus
docs.text:
EE packages Sentaurus with its other course software for the Caddyshack Desktop. Start a Caddyshack Desktop in OnDemand and follow EE's instructions for starting Sentaurus. See Use Caddyshack for EE Courses.

EE's copy of the software is in /home/classes/ee/admin/software, on storage that every FarmShare node can read. To run Sentaurus in a batch job, ask EE how to set it up from there.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
If you used Sentaurus on the old FarmShare, you may have loaded it with a module setup kept in AFS. That setup doesn't work in batch jobs or desktops, because AFS is only available on the login nodes. Use EE's current installation instead.

Sentaurus gets its license from an EE license server. If it reports Cannot connect to license server system., the EE server is usually down or unreachable, often during a network outage. Wait and try again. If it keeps happening, contact EE's IT support.

For questions about Sentaurus itself, contact EE's IT support. For problems with OnDemand or FarmShare, see OnDemand and Desktops.

docs.title: Stata
docs.text: Stata is licensed on FarmShare and comes from the stata module. Run it in an interactive session for exploratory work, or run do-files as batch jobs.

docs.title: Run Stata Interactively
docs.text:
Start an interactive session on a compute node, then load the module and start Stata:

srun --partition=interactive --qos=interactive --cpus-per-task=4 --pty bash
module load stata
stata

You can also run these commands on a login node for small jobs, or in a terminal in a FarmShare Desktop. See Get an Interactive Session.

docs.title: Run a Do-File in a Batch Job
docs.text:
stata-job.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=stata       # (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1      # (2)
#SBATCH --mem=8G               # (3)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00        # (4)

module load stata              # (5)
stata -b do analysis.do        # (6)
  1. A name for the job, shown in squeue.
  2. How many CPU cores the job gets.
  3. How much memory the job gets. Stata keeps your whole dataset in memory, so allow more than the size of the data.
  4. How long the job can run, as hours:minutes:seconds.
  5. Loads the default Stata version. Run module spider stata to see the others.
  6. Runs analysis.do without the interactive prompt. The output goes to analysis.log.

Submit it with sbatch stata-job.sh. See Submit a Batch Job.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
The FarmShare Stata license is shared, and only a few people can run Stata at the same time. If Stata says no license is available, try again later. Close Stata when you're done so the license is free for someone else.

To move your data files onto FarmShare, see Move Files to and from FarmShare.

docs.title: Overview and Timeline
docs.text: Instructors can use FarmShare for a course without asking us for anything, since every student with a full-service SUNet ID can already log in. What we add is shared space, software and capacity for the class, and each of those needs a request from you.

docs.title: What We Can Set Up for a Course
docs.text:
What What it's for Where to read more Course directory and workgroups Shared course files, with staff who can edit them and students who can read them Set Up a Course Class scratch directory Large data sets that the whole class reads Set Up a Course Drop-box folders Students handing in work through the course directory Add Students and TAs Course software Programs the class needs, installed as modules or in the course directory Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes Shared containers One prepared software environment for everyone in the class Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes Reserved nodes or GPUs An assignment or competition that needs guaranteed capacity at a set time Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes

We can also tell you what to expect when the whole class works at once, for example if everyone opens a desktop in the same week. Ask us before you plan an assignment around it.

SRC also has teaching materials on using FarmShare that you can import into your Canvas course. See Teaching Materials.

docs.title: Who Asks
docs.text: Requests for a course usually come from the instructor of record. If a TA asks, we'll check with the instructor and make them the owner. Your TAs can help with the details, and once the course is set up they can manage the student list themselves. See Set Up a Course.

docs.title: When to Ask
docs.text:
Needs Review

Is there a typical lead time for a course setup, software or a reservation that we can give instructors?

Ask as early as you can, before the quarter starts. A course directory is quick to set up. Software, shared containers and reservations take longer, because we install and test them first. The first weeks of each quarter are also our busiest time for support.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
1. Before the quarter starts, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with everything the course needs: the directory, scratch space, software and any reservations. See Set Up a Course for what to include.
  2. Once we've set it up, add your TAs to the staff workgroup and have them add students. See Add Students and TAs.
  3. Test the course software and your assignments on FarmShare yourself, the way students will run them.
  4. Before the first assignment, go through Get Ready for Class Day with your students.

docs.title: Where to Get Help
docs.text:
Needs Review

Does adding "urgent" to the subject change how a request is handled?

Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject. We answer during business hours. If something breaks close to a class, add "urgent" to the subject. See Get Help.

docs.title: Add Students and TAs
docs.text:
Access to a course directory is controlled by the course's two Stanford workgroups. You add TAs to the staff workgroup, and course staff add students to the student workgroup, in Workgroup Manager.

Before you start: the course has to be set up. See Set Up a Course.

docs.title: Who Manages Which Workgroup
docs.text:
Workgroup Members Managed by farmshare:<dept>-<number>-staff You and your TAs or CAs You farmshare:<dept>-<number> Your students Anyone in the staff workgroup

On FarmShare, the workgroups show up as groups named farmshare_<dept>-<number>-staff and farmshare_<dept>-<number>. That's the name you see in ls -l output for files in the course directory.

docs.title: Add TAs
docs.text:
1. Go to Workgroup Manager and log in with your SUNet ID.
  2. Open farmshare:<dept>-<number>-staff.
  3. Add each TA by SUNet ID.

TAs in the staff workgroup can change files in the course directory and manage the student workgroup.

docs.title: Add Students
docs.text:
1. In Workgroup Manager, open farmshare:<dept>-<number>.
  2. Add each student by SUNet ID.

Students who were logged in to FarmShare when you added them should log out and log back in, so their new group membership takes effect.

Every student also needs to log in to FarmShare once before they can use OnDemand or submit jobs. Send them Log In for the First Time.

docs.title: Remove Someone
docs.text: Remove them from the workgroup in Workgroup Manager. That ends their access to the course directory. It doesn't affect their own FarmShare account, which stays active for as long as their SUNet ID does.

docs.title: Drop-Box Folders
docs.text: If you want students to hand in work through the course directory, email srcc-support@stanford.edu and describe what you need, for example a folder per student that only that student and course staff can read. We'll set up the permissions with you and help you test them before students start using them.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: If a student is in the workgroup but still can't reach the course directory after logging out and back in, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" in the subject, the student's SUNet ID and the course directory path.

docs.title: Get Ready for Class Day
docs.text: Most problems students hit in the first session on FarmShare can be caught a few days ahead. Go through these checks before a class or assignment that uses FarmShare, and pass the student ones on to your class.

docs.title: Students Have Logged In Once
docs.text: A student's FarmShare account is finished the first time they log in to a login node. Until then, OnDemand apps and jobs fail with Invalid account or account/partition combination. Have every student log in once before the first class, by SSH or through Clusters > FarmShare Shell Access in OnDemand. Log In for the First Time has the steps.

docs.title: Students' Home Directories Aren't Full
docs.text:
When a home directory is full, OnDemand sessions stop right after they start, and jobs fail. Everyone's home directory holds 50 GB, and Python environments and package caches fill it faster than students expect.

A few days before class, have students check their usage on a login node:

du -sh ~

du reports sizes in GiB, so a full home directory shows as about 48G. If it's close to that, Check and Free Up Space shows how to clear it. For course data sets, use the course directory or class scratch space rather than copies in each student's home directory.

docs.title: The Software Works
docs.text: Run the assignment on FarmShare yourself, the way students will: the same modules, the same OnDemand app, the same desktop size. Software can change between quarters, and a missing module is much easier for us to fix a week before class than on the day. If something is missing, see Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

docs.title: There's Room for Everyone
docs.text:
OnDemand desktops and other interactive sessions share a pool of compute nodes with everyone else on FarmShare. A class of students usually fits, but FarmShare is busiest in the weeks before exams and near deadlines, and sessions can wait in the queue then.

To help students get started:

  • Recommend the smallest desktop size that works for the assignment. Smaller sessions start sooner.
  • Tell students they can leave a request in the queue and ask OnDemand to email them when it starts.
  • Students can check how busy FarmShare is in OnDemand under Clusters > System Status before they start a session.

If you expect the whole class to work at the same time, ask us what to expect.

docs.title: GPUs Are Reserved If You Need Them
docs.text: FarmShare has 24 GPUs for everyone, and batch jobs that ask for GPUs are scheduled ahead of interactive sessions. If students need a GPU in a desktop or interactive session, the wait can be long and hard to predict. For an assignment that depends on GPUs, ask us to reserve some for the class. See Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes.

docs.title: Students Connect to the Login Nodes the Right Way
docs.text: The FarmShare Shell Access terminal in OnDemand always opens on the same login node, rice-01. For a class working in terminals at the same time, have students connect with SSH to login.farmshare.stanford.edu instead, which spreads them across the login nodes. Heavy work, such as running a large program for the whole class, belongs in a desktop or an interactive session on a compute node.

docs.title: You Know How to Reach Us
docs.text:
Needs Review

Does adding "urgent" to the subject change how a request is handled?

Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" and "urgent" in the subject if something breaks close to class. We answer during business hours, so a problem reported on a weekend is picked up on the next business day. Outages and maintenance are announced in #farmshare-announce on Slack.

docs.title: Request Course Software or Reserved Nodes
docs.text:
If your course needs software that isn't on FarmShare, or guaranteed capacity for an assignment, the instructor can ask us to install the software or reserve nodes or GPUs for the class. Both take longer to arrange than a course directory, so ask as early as you can, before the quarter starts.

Before you start: check what's already installed with module spider <name>. See Find Installed Software.

docs.title: Course Software
docs.text:
We can install software for a course in one of these ways:

Option Good for A module Software other courses or researchers might also use. Everyone loads it with module load. An install in the course directory Software only your course needs, or a specific version. Your course staff can also install it there themselves. See Install Software Yourself. A shared container A complete environment with many packages, set up once and used by every student in the same way. See Containers.

Programs with a graphical interface run in a FarmShare Desktop in OnDemand. Students open a terminal in the desktop, load the module and start the program.

Needs Review

When course software isn't licensed yet, is "tell us what license your department has or who is paying" the right process?

For commercial software, check Licensed Software first. If what you need isn't licensed on FarmShare yet, tell us what license your department has or who is paying for one.

docs.title: Reserved Nodes and GPUs
docs.text:
Needs Review

What window can a class reservation cover, and how much lead time does it need?

For an assignment, exam or competition that has to run at a set time, we can hold some of FarmShare's nodes or GPUs for your class. A reservation covers a specific window, such as the week or two of an assignment, and while it lasts the reserved resources are kept for your students.

FarmShare has 24 GPUs, shared by everyone. If your students need GPUs at the same time, especially near the end of the quarter, a reservation is the most reliable way to make sure they get them.

Needs Review

What is the class reservation process, and do students use a reservation by adding its name to their jobs?

When a reservation is ready, we'll tell you its name. Students add it to their jobs, for example in a batch script:

#SBATCH --reservation=<name>

docs.title: Ask for Software or a Reservation
docs.text:
Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" and your course number in the subject, and include:

  1. The course number and quarter.
  2. For software: its name, a link to its website, the version you need, and whether it needs a license.
  3. For a reservation: the dates and times, how many students, and what each student needs, such as CPUs, memory or GPUs.
  4. Roughly how many students will use it at once.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
Test the software on FarmShare yourself, the way your students will use it, before the first assignment that needs it. Problems are much easier for us to fix before a deadline than during one.

If you're not sure whether FarmShare can handle the whole class working at once, ask us. We can tell you what to expect and which desktop size or job settings to recommend to students. See also Get Ready for Class Day.

docs.title: Teaching Materials
docs.text: SRC has Canvas modules that teach students how to use FarmShare and high-performance computing in general. You can import them into your own Canvas course, so students have them alongside the rest of the class material.

docs.title: Find the Modules
docs.text:
1. Log in to Canvas.
  2. Open Commons from the menu on the left.
  3. Search for SRC_HPC.

There are several modules, and you can import as many as your course needs. Most of the material is written for FarmShare.

Students and faculty have access to Canvas Commons by default. If you have a staff role in Canvas and don't see Commons, ask the Stanford Canvas office for access.

docs.title: Pages to Send Students
docs.text:
These pages on this site work as a starting point for students who haven't used FarmShare before:

Page What it covers Log In for the First Time Logging in, and the first login every student needs Run Your First Job Submitting and checking a batch job Where to Put Your Files Home, scratch and course directories Start a Desktop Using a desktop in OnDemand Get Help Where to ask for help, and what to include

Older guides to FarmShare from other courses or older Stanford sites may be out of date. Point students to this site instead.

docs.title: Set Up a Course
docs.text:
The instructor of a course can ask for a shared course directory on FarmShare. It comes with two workgroups: one for course staff, who can change the files, and one for students.

Students don't need a course setup to use FarmShare. Anyone with a full-service SUNet ID can log in and use it for coursework. A course setup is only needed for shared course files.

docs.title: What the Setup Includes
docs.text:
When we set up a course, we create a directory for it at /home/classes/<dept>/<number>, for example /home/classes/cs/101. You own the directory.

We also create two Stanford workgroups for the course:

Workgroup Who belongs in it Who manages it farmshare:<dept>-<number>-staff You and your TAs or CAs You farmshare:<dept>-<number> Your students Your course staff

Your course staff can add and change files in the course directory. Everyone else can read them, including other FarmShare users as well as your students. If some files shouldn't be visible outside the class, such as solutions or student data, say so in your request and we'll set up permissions with you.

Because the staff workgroup manages the student workgroup, your TAs can add and remove students themselves.

If you need scratch space for the course, for large datasets that students all read, ask for a class scratch directory at the same time.

docs.title: Ask for a Course Setup
docs.text:
Requests usually come from the instructor of record for the course. If a TA asks, we'll check with the instructor and make them the owner. If your TA is handling the details, you can send the request yourself and copy them.

Email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare course setup" in the subject, and include:

  1. The course number and quarter, for example CS 101, Winter 2027.
  2. The SUNet IDs of anyone who should be in the staff workgroup.
  3. Whether you'll need class scratch space, course software, or reserved nodes for an assignment.

Ask as early as you can, before the quarter starts. The first weeks of each quarter are our busiest time, and course software and reserved nodes take longer to arrange than a directory does. See Request course software or reserved nodes.

docs.title: After We Set It Up
docs.text:
Add your TAs to the staff workgroup, and have them add students to the student workgroup, in Workgroup Manager.

Each student also needs to log in to FarmShare once before the first assignment. The first login finishes creating their account, and until then OnDemand and job submission won't work for them. Send them Log in for the first time.

Students keep their own work in their home or scratch directories. If you want students to hand in work through the course directory, ask us for drop-box folders, and we'll set up permissions for them. See Add students and TAs.

docs.title: If Something Goes Wrong Before Class
docs.text:
Needs Review

Does adding "urgent" to the subject change how a request is handled?

If something breaks close to a class or a deadline, email srcc-support@stanford.edu with "FarmShare" and "urgent" in the subject. Our support hours are business days, so problems reported on a weekend are picked up on the next business day. Get ready for class day has a checklist of common problems to check for in advance.
